segments.text: It's that time of the year when New York becomes world's geopolitical capital with the annual pinup, the United Nations General Assembly meeting.
This year it's the 81st and happening amid a particularly unstable period with the Ukraine and Iran wars and the global energy crisis.
The agenda is wide ranging, but one question looms large.
Can a UN struggling to respond to today's conflicts reform itself for today's world?
For India, the spotlight will be on S. Jayashankar's address on September 26, with New Delhi expected to renew its push for reform of the Security Council and a permanent seat.
And before India takes the floor, Donald Trump is set to address the general debate on September 22.
That's Tuesday.
That shall be keenly watched.
What next on the mind of the American president after Greenland?
The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opened on the 8th of September.
But the diplomatic spotlight really now shifts to the high-level general debate where world leaders will lay out their priorities from September 22nd to September 28th.
This year's United Nations General Assembly comes at a time when the credibility and effectiveness of the multilateral system itself is under growing discussion.
The official theme itself points to the central challenge, restoring trust while managing a rapidly changing world.
Climate action and just transition.
The right to development.
sea level rise, pandemic preparedness and nuclear disarmament will all feature during the high level week.

But running through these discussions will be the larger question of whether the United Nations can become more effective in dealing with a world that looks very different from the one it was in 1945.
The 81st UNGA is taking place in a specific geopolitical context.
On one hand, you have these various conflicts that are taking place.
The Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Iran-US war that is taking place, and the consequent oil spikes which are impacting the developing economy.
So therefore, there will be some discussion on these things, if not directly on these conflicts, but indirectly there will be reference to.
But at a broader level, if you notice, there are two conflicting dynamics that are at play with reference to multilateralism.
One, the United Nations has not been able to respond and other bodies have not been able to respond to these conflicts and they have not been successful in addressing them.
But at the same time,

There is also a growing demand to reform the United Nations Security Council because there is a perception that you cannot address these conflicts without having new members who can bridge the fault lines.
The ongoing US-Israel-Iran conflict will also be among the key challenges confronting the United Nations.
UNGA can debate the conflict, call for a ceasefire and back diplomatic efforts.
But its resolutions are non-binding, meaning the General Assembly can build political pressure but cannot itself force the parties to end the fighting.
So the question is whether UNGA 81 can turn diplomatic discussion into pressure for de-escalation.
While India's immediate diplomatic calendar also includes its campaign for a non-permanent Security Council seat for 2028-29.
The larger long-term objective remains a permanent seat at the Council's table and the argument is not being made only by India.
India, Japan, Germany and Brazil, the G4 have jointly pushed for an expanded Security Council with permanent representation for themselves.
India's push for a permanent security council has been going on for quite a while and nobody supports it because they don't want another country coming into it.
This is that old Bretton Woods institution which has transformed itself into a security council which is completely and 100% unrepresentative of the reality of the world as it is today.

But so the hurdle is quite simple is that once you you know they don't want a country which is as non-aligned and you know we operate independently we have no particular regard to A or B or C so they don't want that kind of a country.
The US itself may they will every all of them will give lip service that oh yeah India should join it is this and that but that's where it stops.
Do I see this changing?
No I don't.

That is the central challenge for India's permanent seat campaign as their demand for reform may have gathered momentum but changing the composition of the Security Council requires political agreement among UN member states including the existing permanent powers.
India has also sought to build a wider coalition around the reform question.
At the 2026 BRIC Summit in New Delhi, the Delhi declaration reiterated support for comprehensive UN reform and called for greater representation of developing countries in the Security Council.
The declaration also recorded support from China and Russia for aspirations of Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.
But political backing on paper is one thing and actual reform is another and that gap is precisely what UNGA could put under the spotlight.
Not only that, the BRICS New Delhi Declaration also clearly stated that countries such as Brazil and India should be made members.
And also some of the African countries can also be considered for permanent membership of the United Nations Security Council.
So there is slowly momentum that is, there is a growing momentum to reform the United Nations Security Council.
And that is going to be one of the principal agendas
for India in terms of reforming the multilateral institutions.
We should remember precisely at a time when multilateral institutions are under stress.
It should be noted that if there is a country that should be part of United Nations Security Council, expanded membership of the United Nations Security Council, it should be India.
For India, therefore, the argument is not restricted to demand for status.
As New Delhi has repeatedly linked its claims to its role in UN peacekeeping, its engagement with the Global South and its wider push for reform of multilateral institutions.
Brixi is definitely playing a role in reshaping, for example, to an extent, how IMF operates, how the World Bank operates, the kind of financial systems in which all these countries are operating in.
And these are all countries who need this kind of, you know, less stringent financial loans and things, so they are okay.
But when it comes to coming back to the UN Security Council reform, China themselves, though they talk about it, they will not support India.
They haven't even supported South Africa.
So, if you talk of real politics, the Global South should have a separate, what shall I say, a pressure point, maybe a separate organization.
So as the reform debate unfolds, the focus will not simply be on who supports the idea, but on whether that support can create enough momentum for negotiations to move forward.
Donald Trump is scheduled to address the general debate on September 22nd, where he is expected to highlight what he describes as diplomatic and peace efforts undertaken during his second term.
His address is also expected to touch on America's approach to sovereignty, security and the role of multilateral institutions.
Trump's UNGA week will also coincide with another closely watched issue – Greenland.
After months of pressure over the strategic Arctic territory, Trump has announced a deal with Denmark to expand the military presence in Greenland.
The deal keeps Greenland within the Kingdom of Denmark, while Washington says it gives the United States permanent control over security and allows for an expanded military presence.
Donald Trump tries to sell it as a wind.
He obviously didn't
get in this agreement what he originally set out to have that is sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States.
But can the UN General Assembly intervene in the Greenland issue?
UNGA can discuss questions of sovereignty, territorial integrity and self-determination.
But it cannot overturn a bilateral security agreement between US, Denmark and Greenland.
The original 1951 agreement covered a lot of different bases in Greenland.
There's a number of amending agreements limiting the current American presence to only the one Bitufik or Tule space base.
So if he wants actually the American military wants to expand
there would be needs to be consent from Denmark at Greenland.
That would have been given under the old agreement, but he can claim it as a win also.
And then, of course, the important expansion substantially in this agreement would be the investment screening, whatever provision is there, because that's not at all covered in the 1951 agreement.
Four days later, it will be India's turn.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar is scheduled to address the general debate on the afternoon of September 26th.
The main reason why India should join the UN Security Council is not just about status.
It is about bringing up issues which are extremely important to the global south and particularly our area.
You know, for example, climate change.
You saw the devastation in Nepal.

you saw the issue of you know they will impose you know tell you that you need to pay for climate change when i have not contributed to climate change and neither has much of the global south so these are all things which needs a more equitable balance so that
The global economy can grow.
I mean, these countries sitting down and telling each other what to do doesn't help the global economy and they depend on the global economy revival as well.
You haven't actually recovered since Covid.
You want actual recovery, you have to make sure the markets where you sell and those countries with resources which you use also have a better deal.
Otherwise, this is not going to work.
UNGA 81 will therefore be about much more than a series of speeches.

It will be a test of how the world's powers respond to a changing geopolitical landscape and whether calls for a more representative United Nations can move from the General Assembly floor to the negotiating table.
